_about: Field terms for F23, same shape as papers/glossary.json.

mycorrhiza.definition: a root tip of a plant enclosed by a fungus that lives with it, the fungus taking sugars from the plant and passing it water and soil nutrients; here the tuberculate root tips that Rhizopogon fungi form on Douglas-fir
mycorrhiza.excludes: fungi that rot wood or cause disease, and fungal threads in the soil away from a root

genet.definition: one genetic individual of a fungus, recognised by its microsatellite profile, which may spread through the soil and colonise many root tips
genet.excludes: a species, and a single fungal thread or fruiting body

bipartite-network.definition: a network with two kinds of node, here trees and fungal genets, in which a link joins a tree to a genet found on at least one of its root tips and never joins two nodes of the same kind
bipartite-network.excludes: a network of measured flows between trees

degree.definition: the number of links a node has: the genets on one tree, the trees one genet reaches, or, in the tree-tree view, the other trees that share at least one genet with a tree
degree.excludes: the strength or direction of a link

degree-preserving-null.definition: a control that rewires the links of a network at random while every tree keeps its number of genets and every genet its number of trees, drawn here by the curveball algorithm 1,000 times per plot
degree-preserving-null.excludes: a shuffle that also changes how many links each node has

hub-share.definition: the share of all tree-tree links held by the top 10 percent of trees ranked by their number of tree-tree links
hub-share.excludes: a measure of how much a hub tree passes to others

nodf.definition: the degree to which the partners of poorly linked nodes are a subset of the partners of well linked nodes, scored from 0 to 100 by the NODF index (nestedness based on overlap and decreasing fill)
nodf.excludes: modules, which are groups of nodes linked mostly among themselves

modularity.definition: Newman's Q: how far links fall inside groups of nodes rather than between groups, beyond what random links with the same degrees would give; here the best of 20 Louvain runs
modularity.excludes: spatial clumping of samples, which can produce modules without any network structure

z-score.definition: the real value minus the mean of the control draws, divided by their standard deviation; values beyond 2 in size are rare under the control
z-score.excludes: a p value, and a measure of effect size in the units of the data

power-law.definition: a degree distribution whose tail falls as a fixed power of the degree, so that a few nodes have very many links; a network with such a tail is called scale-free
power-law.excludes: skewed distributions with an exponential tail, which also have a few well linked nodes

aic.definition: the Akaike information criterion, twice the number of fitted parameters minus twice the log-likelihood; between two models fitted to the same data the lower value is preferred, and a gap of 2 or more is the usual bar
aic.excludes: a test that one model is true

spearman.definition: the correlation between the ranks of two quantities, from -1 to 1, which counts any steadily rising or falling relation and is not pulled by single extreme values
spearman.excludes: the slope of a relation, and evidence of cause

partial-rho.definition: the Spearman correlation between two quantities after the ranks of a third, here the number of root tips sampled per tree, have been regressed out of both
partial-rho.excludes: a causal effect, and a correction that is known to be the right size

bootstrap.definition: an interval made by recomputing a number many times on units drawn with replacement from the data, here trees, logs or inventory plots, and keeping the middle 95 percent of the results
bootstrap.excludes: an interval that also covers doubt about the model's form

relative-density.definition: the apparent density of a log tissue at a sampling time divided by the same log's density of that tissue when the log was laid out in 1985
relative-density.excludes: mass loss and carbon loss, which also count the volume a log loses as it fragments

decay-rate.definition: the constant k in the single-exponential model, the fraction of remaining density lost per year; a half-life is the natural log of 2 divided by k
decay-rate.excludes: a rate measured from mass, and the rate in the first years of a lag model

carry-forward.definition: the forecast that a later sampling will show the same mean relative density as the last sampling used for fitting, here year 16
carry-forward.excludes: a forecast from a fitted decay curve

skill.definition: one minus the mean absolute error of a model's forecast divided by the mean absolute error of a baseline on the same held-out logs; 0 means no better than the baseline and 1 means perfect
skill.excludes: a score on the logs used to fit the model

logistic-regression.definition: a model that gives the log odds of a yes-or-no outcome, here recorded wind damage, as a weighted sum of the features; here fitted with an L2 penalty on standardised features
logistic-regression.excludes: a model of how much damage a tree has

odds-ratio.definition: the factor by which the odds of the outcome change when a feature rises by one standard deviation and the other features stay fixed; 1 means no change
odds-ratio.excludes: a ratio of probabilities, and a causal effect

slenderness.definition: tree height divided by stem diameter at breast height, both in the same units
slenderness.excludes: the height-to-diameter ratio measured at the base of the stem

auc.definition: the area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen damaged tree is ranked above a randomly chosen undamaged one, with 0.5 for guessing
auc.excludes: how close the predicted probabilities are to the observed rates

brier-skill.definition: one minus the Brier score of a model divided by the Brier score of always forecasting the base rate, where the Brier score is the mean squared gap between a probability and the outcome coded 0 or 1
brier-skill.excludes: a ranking measure such as AUC, which ignores whether the probabilities are right in size
